domain: Disaster Anthropology / Institutional Memory / Commitment Systems
topic_summary: Analysis of the Aneyoshi tsunami stone's 78-year land-use commitment (1933-2011), examining whether the kernel 'do not build below this point' persisted as live behavioral practice or decayed to commemorative symbol. The 2011 tsunami stopped just below the stone line, validating compliance across three generations while surrounding coastal towns that ignored similar stones were devastated.

key_entities: Aneyoshi village (11 households, maintained stone-line compliance 1933-2011)
Tsunami stone (erected 1933, explicit building prohibition inscription)
Village leadership (Tamishige Kimura, enforced ancestral rule)
Surrounding Sanriku coast towns (rebuilt below stone lines, suffered 2011 casualties)
key_tensions: Live practice vs commemorative symbol (kernel vitality contest)
Economic proximity to fishing vs safety elevation (daily cost of compliance)
Ancient stone warnings vs modern seawall confidence (competing protection paradigms)
key_claims: Aneyoshi maintained 100% compliance with stone-line building restriction 1933-2011
2011 tsunami stopped ~90m below stone line, zero Aneyoshi casualties
Surrounding towns ignored similar stones, suffered devastation
Three-generation memory fade is typical (Imamura), Aneyoshi is exceptional
School education + leadership reinforcement sustained commitment
key_mechanisms: Intergenerational transmission via school curriculum (Yuto Kimura testimony)
Leadership enforcement ('rule no one dares break' - Tamishige Kimura)
Physical inscription permanence (stone as persistent environmental cue)
key_absences: No documented defection attempts or enforcement conflicts in 78-year period
No analysis of what happened to families who might have wanted to build below the line

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The 1933 inscription 'Do not build any homes below this point' as binding land-use constraint
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Ancestral trauma (double devastation 1896/1933) + village leadership enforcement + institutional memory (school system)
commitment_system_recognition.kernel_collapse_reason: The supposed 'commemorative-husk vs behavioral-competence' contest is not a genuine kernel contest. Both readings agree on what the constraint IS (a building prohibition below the stone line). They disagree only on whether Aneyoshi COMPLIED with that constraint. This is an empirical question about adherence, not a structural question about what the kernel constrains. The 2011 outcome decisively resolves the empirical question: Aneyoshi complied (behavioral-competence reading validated). There is no interpretive plurality here—just one constraint with contested compliance status, now settled by catastrophe-theorem break (D5). The readings collapse to a single axis: commitment_persistence_under_generational_turnover.

axes.structural_delta: Mechanisms that sustain behavioral compliance with ancestral land-use prohibition across three generations (78 years) despite economic costs and absence of catastrophe reinforcement
axes.primary_observable: Building location compliance rate 1933-2011; institutional memory transmission mechanisms (school curriculum, leadership rhetoric); defection rate
axes.selection_reason: Core analytical target: the rope mechanisms (school transmission, leadership enforcement, physical inscription) that prevented the typical three-generation memory fade

axes.structural_delta: Double devastation (1896, 1933) within single lifetime as foundational legitimacy for the stone-line prohibition
axes.primary_observable: Historical casualty counts; temporal proximity of dual catastrophes; inscription content referencing 'calamity of great tsunamis'
axes.selection_reason: Upstream mountain: the physical/historical substrate that grounds the kernel's authority. Without dual catastrophe, no stone; without stone, no commitment to analyze.

axes.structural_delta: Seawall construction as competing protection paradigm that enabled surrounding towns to defect from stone-line compliance while Aneyoshi maintained adherence
axes.primary_observable: Seawall construction timeline vs building-below-stone-line rates in surrounding towns; 2011 casualty differential between Aneyoshi and defector towns
axes.selection_reason: Downstream synthesis: the tangled_rope that explains why Aneyoshi is exceptional. Seawalls provided rationalization for defection elsewhere; Aneyoshi's rope mechanisms resisted this gradient.

axes.selection_reason: Deferred: economic cost is real but structurally redundant with commitment_persistence analysis. The rope mechanisms already account for sustained compliance despite costs.

axes.selection_reason: Deferred: physical permanence is one mechanism among several (school, leadership). Captured within commitment_persistence rope analysis rather than requiring separate axis.

deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Structurally redundant with commitment_persistence_under_generational_turnover. The rope mechanisms already account for sustained compliance despite economic costs.

omegas.description: No documented defection attempts in 78 years. Were there families who wanted to build below the line? If so, what enforcement mechanisms prevented it? If not, what explains unanimous internalization? The absence of conflict data leaves the coercion/consent balance unresolved.

The supposed kernel contest (commemorative-husk vs behavioral-competence) collapses under scrutiny. Both readings agree on what the constraint is; they disagree only on whether Aneyoshi complied. The 2011 outcome settles this empirically. Not a genuine interpretive plurality—just contested adherence, now resolved.

Why did other Sanriku coast towns with similar stones defect while Aneyoshi complied? The research notes 'many' stones were ignored but provides no systematic comparison of stone characteristics, inscription content, or local institutional structures. The modernization_defection_gradient axis hypothesizes seawalls as rationalization, but the mechanism of differential defection remains underspecified.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan) + comparative context gap

omegas.description: The 2011 tsunami occurred 78 years after stone placement—just beyond Imamura's 'three generation' memory fade threshold. Was this timing coincidental, or does it suggest the commitment was approaching fragility? If the tsunami had occurred in 2031 (98 years), would compliance have held?

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. The kernel collapse (commemorative-husk vs behavioral-competence) is not a protocol failure—it is the correct application of §1.3-K's kernel/not-kernel decision. The readings do not instantiate different constraints; they contest adherence to one constraint. The 2011 catastrophe-theorem break (D5) decisively resolves the empirical question, leaving no interpretive plurality to decompose.
